title: ILTA EVOLVE: AI, Cybersecurity, and Data Governance
author: Josh Smith · Ken Jones · Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source narrowly encourages skills preparation and conference participation, which is compatible with the cluster’s emphasis on readiness and engagement. However, it offers no developed position on user-led adoption, AI capability, verification, autonomy or market uncertainty, so there is insufficient evidence that it accepts the cluster’s principal proposition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, governed adoption rather than blanket deployment or avoidance. It emphasises practical experimentation, use-case evidence, security-conscious product selection, data guardrails and education, while recognising model differences and fast-changing capabilities. This aligns with the cluster’s view that value depends on context-specific deployment and governance, though it provides limited evidence on verification, task-level performance or operating-model redesign.
qs: So all those topics have opened up and we have sessions on those that evolved this year that I think are really beneficial, including a workshop about AI governance and how to make sure that when you're selecting an AI product for your firm, you're doing it in a security minded conscientious way.

kp.k: Personal experimentation can support responsible professional AI adoption
kp.d: In the conversation recorded February 25th, 2025, Abramowitz recommends using AI personally before using it professionally to develop an understanding of possible applications with fewer client-data and compliance concerns. Jones supports this recommendation from his own teaching and travel-planning experience, arguing that iterative prompting and reflection on privacy help users prepare for professional adoption. These are practitioner experiences and recommendations, not measured learning outcomes.
qs: before you use it at work, use it in your personal life because by using it in your personal life, you're going to open up your imagination to what's possible at work.
The more you use it personally and embrace that technology, the easier and better job you'll do applying those frameworks to work.

kp.k: Security AI augments analysts and redirects their work
kp.d: Smith reports that his firm benefits from using Copilot for Security to analyse logs and assemble incident information that would otherwise take a level one analyst probably an hour or two. He says this lets analysts undertake more beneficial work and develop their careers. He anticipates a broader workload shift, explicitly favouring augmentation rather than replacing people, including potential resource savings for smaller firms. The time estimate is anecdotal; no systematic productivity measurement is supplied.
qs: One way that we've really found some benefit is using Copilot for Security to analyze logs, analyze situations to give us that output that it would take a level one analyst, probably an hour, two hours, to grab all that information and put it together and make a story.
That's let our level one analyst level up per se and do things that are better for their career paths and their lives and better for the firm.

I don't want to replace them because I don't want to replace people, but you're augmenting that workload to where those humans can do other things that are more beneficial, especially for even smaller firms.

kp.k: Client guidelines increasingly encourage responsible AI efficiency
kp.d: Smith reports encountering both outside counsel guidelines that prohibit AI use with client data and newer guidelines expecting responsible use to save fees and time. He also recounts clients asking about the firm's AI practices so they can apply them within their own corporate legal environments. He interprets these encounters as an emerging change in client attitudes, not as evidence of universal acceptance or quantified market adoption.
qs: We're seeing this in outside council guidelines, but we're seeing some newer issued guidelines that say, we expect you to use AI responsibly to save on fees, to use it responsibly, to save time, and to be more efficient when doing work for us.
we want to know what you're doing, so we can do that ourselves, and how to do things in our corporate law environment to where we can be more efficient.

kp.k: Governance should enable adoption rather than blanket prohibition
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that blanket non-adoption on information-security and governance grounds is not sustainable, while acknowledging concerns about LLM opacity and rejecting reckless use. Smith agrees that education and appropriate data guardrails are necessary. The discussion identifies confidentiality, privacy, bias, hallucination and third-party risk as relevant concerns, but provides no specific legal rule interpretation or measured risk assessment.
qs: as much as we don't want people to be reckless with their use of AI, I think we're at the place in history where if you have talked to yourself into non adoption of AI because of information security and information governance and everything that goes along with it, I don't think you're doing it right.
Then guardrails, the appropriate guardrails around what you do with your data to be responsible.
where do we let our data go? And what happens to it when we put it in an AI LLM and making sure that the data is secure within the firm?

kp.k: Local models broaden deployment choices beyond commercial cloud
kp.d: Abramowitz suggests that DeepSeek challenges assumptions that access to capable models requires moving entirely to commercial cloud services, potentially enabling a mix of cloud, on-premises, small-model and open-source deployments. Smith describes local experimentation and private Azure deployments, and suggests in-house development may be less expensive than previously expected. He qualifies his enthusiasm with an anecdotal observation that his local model follows some instructions less well than alternatives; this is not a formal benchmark or cost study.
qs: We can be in the cloud where we want to be, and we can be on-prem where we want to be and run small language models, run open source models that may have felt like even a few months ago, we're not going to really be an option.
We can start developing some of these things in-house and in our data centers and do some of this on-prem because it's not going to be as expensive as we thought it would be.
It's like, well, here's what I think and I'm going to disregard what you told me on some of it.

kp.k: AI supply spans incumbent software and specialist startups
kp.d: Jones describes established document-management and legal-research companies embedding AI within their products, alongside startups developing new applications. He presents private, secure use within firms' own environments as part of the incumbents' approach. This is a qualitative account of the legal-technology supplier landscape, not evidence about vendor market shares or alternative legal service providers delivering legal work.

kp.k: Technical literacy can improve AI procurement decisions
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that legal professionals need foundational understanding of AI and LLMs, including technical details, to distinguish product categories, relevant outputs and KPIs. He proposes using that understanding to clarify business requirements and choose between startups, internal development and existing firm software. Smith likewise argues that deeper technical understanding enables better governance and ethical questions. These are educational recommendations and intended outcomes, not demonstrated procurement results.

there are a lot of companies that are AI products, but they do different things. And the outputs, the KPIs, are different kind of based on what you're doing.

here's where I need to be working with a startup. Here's where I need to be developing my own product. Here's where I probably have a product already at my firm that does this. I don't need anything new.

kp.k: Business operations offer AI entry points beyond legal practice
kp.d: Jones identifies pricing, collections, timekeeping and legal drafting as areas of AI application being explored by startups. Abramowitz argues that firms may find it easier to begin with business operations than with automating highly trained attorneys' substantive work, while not rejecting practice applications. The discussion identifies opportunities rather than establishing realised financial returns, changes in fee models or lawyer displacement.
qs: one is a session focused on the application of AI to legal finance, topics like pricing, collections, improved timekeeping, getting the entries into systems easier.
There's a lot of startups in the legal drafting, and one of them proposed a session in that area.
I always feel like they're probably like an easier place to start with a lot of firms and like, look at the business of the law firm and how can we apply AI to the business of the law firm side.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The speakers describe AI as augmenting law-firm operations, changing client expectations and technology procurement, and expanding deployment options rather than necessarily replacing people.
pts.d: Josh Smith reports that his firm's use of Copilot for Security synthesizes logs and situations that would otherwise require a level-one analyst approximately one or two hours to assemble into a narrative. He says this enables analysts to undertake more beneficial work and predicts a wider workload shift, explicitly favoring augmentation over replacement, with time and resource benefits for smaller firms. Smith also reports a shift in some clients' outside counsel guidelines toward expecting responsible AI use to reduce fees and improve efficiency; some clients ask about the firm's AI practices to apply them in their own corporate legal environments. Ken Jones describes established document-management and legal-research vendors embedding AI in their products, including private Azure-based deployments, alongside startup activity. Zach Abramowitz argues that law-firm business functions can be an easier starting point than automating sophisticated substantive legal work; he and Jones identify pricing, collections, timekeeping and drafting as application areas. Abramowitz argues that DeepSeek and open-source or smaller models make selective on-premises deployment more plausible, reducing the perceived need to move everything to commercial cloud models. Smith similarly describes opportunities for internal development and local deployment at lower anticipated cost, while also describing private Azure deployments. Abramowitz argues that blanket non-adoption on information-security grounds is not sustainable, while Smith stresses education and responsible data guardrails. Finally, Abramowitz predicts that better foundational AI knowledge will improve vendor selection and help firms distinguish when to buy from a startup, develop internally or use an existing product.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily practitioner experience, client anecdotes, product examples and expectations for education; no systematic study or benchmark is supplied.
pts.d: Smith's cybersecurity productivity claim is grounded in reported workplace use, with an approximate estimate of the human assembly time displaced, not a measured AI completion time or formal before-and-after study. His account of changing buyer expectations rests on outside counsel guidelines and client conversations, without identifying clients, reproducing guidelines or quantifying prevalence. His deployment claims draw on experimentation with Azure and locally run models, including informal comparisons of outputs and instruction-following. Jones draws on his legal-technology experience, observations of established vendors and startups, and conference programming. Abramowitz names Lexpipe in matter pricing and ODDR in finance and collections as examples, without giving verified performance or commercial results. His claims that business operations are an easier entry point, that blanket non-adoption is unsustainable, and that technical education improves purchasing are judgments or predictions rather than measured findings. Jones and Smith also cite their own personal experimentation as supporting the view that familiarity helps workplace adoption. The episode is partly promotional for ILTA EVOLVE; anticipated workshop benefits and proposed sessions should be distinguished from demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims are anchored to February 25, 2025: current adoption and experimentation, an emerging client-expectation shift, and near-term but mostly undated predictions.
pts.d: The conversation explicitly identifies its recording date as February 25, 2025. Smith describes cybersecurity benefits as already occurring and contrasts his current AI use with the previous year's conference. The broader workplace shift is prospective, with no deadline or quantified employment forecast. Changing outside counsel expectations are described as beginning to emerge, not universal: Smith acknowledges continued restrictive guidelines alongside newer permissive or affirmative ones. Claimed cost and efficiency advantages are conditioned on responsible use, data stewardship and appropriate guardrails. Abramowitz frames on-premises alternatives as becoming more plausible within the preceding few months, not as demonstrating that every workload can move off cloud services. Smith qualifies local-model enthusiasm by reporting weaker instruction-following in his own tests than with other models. Procurement improvements are expected from education and workshops at the April 27–30, 2025 conference, not presented as established results. Jones's personal-to-professional learning claim is conditioned on repeated use, contextual prompting and attention to confidentiality, bias, hallucination and privacy.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law-firm cybersecurity and technology staff, firm business teams, lawyers, corporate clients and AI vendors.
pts.d: For level-one cybersecurity analysts, Smith describes less time spent assembling information and greater scope for career-enhancing tasks, rather than an announced reduction in headcount. Smaller firms are identified as potential beneficiaries of saved time and resources. Law-firm IT, governance, risk, compliance and procurement personnel face new questions about data movement, product security, hosting arrangements, ethical considerations and build-versus-buy choices. Finance and administrative teams are potential users of pricing, collections and timekeeping applications; practicing lawyers are users of research, document-management and drafting tools. Corporate clients are described both as buyers seeking lower fees and more efficient outside-counsel work and as prospective adopters learning from their firms' approaches. Established legal-technology vendors and startups offer different routes to implementation, while internal development is presented as another option. The source does not make a concrete prediction about associate staffing structures, partner leverage, law-firm ownership, widespread lawyer unemployment or access to justice.
